rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.2-2.3 and 3 - the authors monitored soil water content with TDR tubes, crop height, LAI, root distribution, groundwater level and meteorology in three flood-irrigated maize fields for one growth season (2013) and ran HYDRUS-1D calibrated and validated against the measured SWC (Fig. 4, RMSE 0.010-0.054). Q2: Section 3.3 and Table 2 - with the validated model, scenario schedules OI-1 and OI-2 reduced irrigation by 65/45/13% and 84/61/23% in NFW/OF/NFD while Ta/Tp was maintained or increased and deep percolation and evaporation were reduced; Section 4.4 reports Ta/(P+I) rising from 0.79, 0.48, 0.64 to 1.75, 0.83, 0.74 (OI-1). Q4: Sections 3.2-3.3, Table 2, Fig. 5 - the intermediate variables (drainage at the lower boundary, capillary rise, soil evaporation, relative transpiration Ta/Tp, soil water content) are modelled and partly measured, showing that savings arise from cutting deep percolation (e.g. D reduced by 428, 329, 162 mm under OI-2). Q5: Sections 2.1 and 3.3, Table 2, Fig. 9 - three fields with distinct soil profiles and groundwater conditions (loamy OF with deep GWL, sandy NFD with deep GWL, sandy-over-loam NFW with shallow GWL), with irrigation reductions and schedules reported separately for each. Q7: Abstract, Sections 4.3-4.4, Conclusions - the authors state that soil texture and GWL must be considered: sandy NFD requires frequent (12) small (25-50 mm) irrigations, loamy OF fewer (6) larger ones; the large saving in NFW depends on capillary rise from shallow groundwater; plastic film is described as necessary for water saving; secondary salinisation must be watched given slightly saline groundwater. Q8: Section 4.4 - limitations stated: no feedback of root water uptake on crop growth (same growth indexes in all scenarios), no feedback of rescheduled irrigation on GWL in NFW, which probably overestimated groundwater contribution and water-saving potential; Section 4.1 notes SWC overestimation after irrigation and 1-D simplification of mulch.
rows.notes: The water-saving effect of the optimized schedules is a scenario-simulation result from a model calibrated/validated on measured SWC in the same fields; the optimized schedules themselves were never implemented or measured in the field, so Q2 is a lenient yes. Single season (2013), single region (Heihe basin). Only one method (model), so Q3 no. Only RMSE/MAE validation errors and p-values for correlation; no dispersion or uncertainty propagation for the saving estimates (Q9 no). The technology label 'app_scheduling' is broader than the study, which uses a HYDRUS-1D numerical model rather than a software app, but the passage text describes exactly what the study did, so no mismatch flagged.

notes: Full text appears complete. Study is a one-season field monitoring plus HYDRUS-1D modelling of three flood-irrigated maize fields; optimized schedules are proposed from scenario simulation only.
